title: Can religion bridge ethnic divides? How pastors in the DRC promote collective action where chiefs cannot: Guest post by Gabriel Granato
gist: Job-market paper (Gabriel Granato, UC Berkeley) RCT with 1,040 residents in 336 salongo community-labor teams in Kananga, DRC: chiefs raise participation ~6 p.p. only in ethnically homogeneous teams via social enforcement, while Pentecostal pastors raise it ~5.8 p.p. only in mixed teams via internalized religious motives; community labor equaled ~$28,000, nearly a third of provincial property-tax receipts.

insights.claim: A randomized study in Kananga, DRC, assigned salongo community-labor teams to include a chief, a pastor or no leader, and varied ethnic homogeneity, covering 1,040 participants across 336 teams.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rigorous evidence on informal governance in fragile states.

insights.claim: In leaderless teams residents participated on roughly half of possible days, about 13 hours per week, with no difference between ethnically homogeneous and mixed teams, so ethnic cohesion alone did not raise participation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Challenges the assumption that ethnic diversity per se undermines collective action.
insights.quote: ethnic cohesion alone did not improve participation
insights.locator: Ethnic diversity changed who could organize

themes.theme: Chiefs vs pastors: who can mobilize whom

insights.claim: Chiefs increased public-works participation by 6 percentage points in ethnically homogeneous teams but had little effect in mixed teams, while pastors raised participation 5.8 points in mixed teams with no detectable effect in homogeneous teams.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Choice of local implementation partner should depend on community ethnic composition.
insights.quote: Chiefs increased participation by 6 percentage points in homogeneous teams but had little effect in mixed teams.
insights.locator: Ethnic diversity changed who could organize

insights.claim: In homogeneous teams pastors' influence is negative where ethnic attachment is strong, suggesting religious appeals may be displaced by stronger ethnic obligations, whereas in mixed teams pastors become more effective as ethnic identification strengthens.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Religious institutions work as bridging capital precisely where ethnic division is salient.
insights.locator: For pastors, ethnic attachment matters differently

insights.claim: Pastors' effects are concentrated among residents who treat religion as a guiding principle.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Pentecostal networks' mobilizing power depends on religiosity depth.

themes.theme: Mechanisms: social enforcement vs internalized obligation

insights.claim: Chiefs' positive effects were concentrated where individual participation was disclosed at team meetings, consistent with enforcement through social accountability.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Traditional authority relies on observability; transparency tools amplify it.
insights.locator: Chiefs’ positive effects in homogeneous teams

insights.claim: Pastors raised participation in mixed teams without individual disclosure, but their effect fell toward zero when contributions became public, contrary to a social-pressure mechanism.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Mixing religious appeals with public monitoring can backfire.
insights.quote: their estimated effect fell toward zero when contributions became public
insights.locator: Chiefs’ positive effects in homogeneous teams

insights.claim: Chiefs rely on external incentives enforced through social accountability while pastors appeal to internalized religious obligations.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Distinct levers for designing community-driven development programs.

themes.theme: Community labor as local fiscal capacity

insights.claim: Across 28 neighborhoods covering about 14% of Kananga households, residents supplied 70,250 hours across an estimated 832 worksites, with contributions worth roughly $28,000, nearly a third of provincial 2025 property-tax receipts.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Informal labor contributions are a material fiscal resource in weak states.

insights.so_what: Program design in fragmented cities should leverage cross-cutting institutions like churches.
